title: Meh-conomy or Momentum? Stagnant Jobs and Stubborn Inflation Collide Before the Midterms
subtitle: The July jobs report showed an unexpected loss of 23,000 jobs while inflation remained elevated at 3.4%, setting up a contentious debate over economic momentum ahead of the midterms.

conservative.headline: Wages Growing Fastest Since the 1980s as Trump Economy Absorbs Global Energy Shock
conservative.byline: As seen on Fox News, Breitbart, Fox Business
paragraphs: The American economy continues to deliver historic wage gains for workers even as it absorbs the shock of a global energy crisis sparked by Iran's aggression, with real earnings rising at rates not seen since the Reagan era.

White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett affirmed that "the economy continues to be strong" despite July's unexpected jobs data. The fundamentals remain solid: wage growth is outpacing inflation, manufacturing is experiencing a renaissance, and private sector productivity continues to climb.

According to Breitbart's analysis, real average weekly wages rose 1.9% through early 2026, marking the highest rate since March 2021. In the manufacturing sector specifically, wage growth consistently exceeded 4 percent, with productivity gains driving real income increases that benefit working-class Americans.

The July jobs number, while showing a technical loss, reflects what economists describe as a "balanced slowdown" in labor supply and demand adjusting in tandem. This is not a collapse but a normalization after years of extraordinary pandemic-era distortions.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh, delivering his closely watched Jackson Hole speech in late August, made clear that "it is the Fed's job to deliver stable prices" and signaled his willingness to take action if needed. His disciplined approach has restored credibility to an institution that lost its way under the previous administration's inflationary spending spree.

The inflation picture, while not perfect, shows an economy absorbing a major external shock. Yes, gas prices rose when Trump acted decisively against Iranian aggression, but that temporary spike is the price of standing up to a rogue regime rather than appeasing it. Core economic fundamentals—wage growth, manufacturing output, private sector dynamism—remain robust.

The bottom line: American workers are experiencing the fastest real wage growth in a generation, and the economy is successfully weathering a global energy crisis that would have crippled weaker nations. That's not a "meh-conomy"—that's American resilience.

liberal.headline: Job Losses Mount and Inflation Stays Elevated as Americans Buy Groceries on Credit
liberal.byline: As seen on CNN, Daily Beast, NPR
paragraphs: The American economy is delivering a brutal one-two punch to working families: jobs are disappearing while prices remain stubbornly high, forcing millions to put groceries and rent on credit cards just to survive.

The grim reality is that "wages were up 3.5% while inflation is up 4.2%", meaning workers are actually losing ground every month. As the Daily Beast reported, "working Americans increasingly report that their paychecks can't keep up with Trump's high prices". This isn't economic anxiety—this is mathematical reality.

The jobs picture is equally bleak. CNN's economic analysis captured what economists are calling a "soft job market AND elevated inflation" scenario, the worst of both worlds. The Federal Reserve typically faces one problem or the other—now it's facing both simultaneously, with no easy policy tools to fix either.

NPR's reporting underscored the squeeze on family budgets, noting that "most people's paychecks aren't keeping pace" with rising prices, even as the job market weakens. Gas prices are over $4 per gallon thanks to Trump's reckless decision to escalate conflict with Iran, and the Fed is powerless to bring those costs down.

The human cost shows up in the credit data: credit card debt hit $1.26 trillion in the second quarter, with delinquency rates at levels not seen since the Great Recession. A survey found that 55% of Americans are using credit cards for basic necessities like groceries, rent, and utilities.

LendingTree's chief credit analyst Matt Schulz explained that "people are looking for ways to extend their budget in the face of stubborn inflation". Translation: Americans are going into debt to afford the basics while Wall Street celebrates wage statistics that don't reflect their lived reality.

Meanwhile, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole speech signaled he's prepared to raise interest rates even as jobs disappear—making mortgages, car loans, and credit card debt even more expensive for struggling families. His priority is "stable prices" for bondholders, not jobs for workers.

The bottom line: This is a meh-conomy at best and a recession in disguise at worst, with working families paying the price for Trump's foreign policy failures and the Fed's indifference to Main Street pain.

factcheck.headline: Separating Fact from Spin
paragraphs: Both sides are cherry-picking data to support predetermined narratives about an economy that's genuinely complicated. Here's what we actually know.
THE UNDISPUTED FACTS:

✓ Jobs data: The economy shed 23,000 jobs in July, the first monthly loss since the pandemic recovery. Previous months were revised downward by 103,000 jobs combined. The August report is expected to show modest gains of 50,000-58,000 positions.

✓ Inflation data: The Consumer Price Index showed inflation stood at 3.4% in July, down slightly from 3.5% in June but well above the Fed's 2% target. Core inflation (excluding food and energy) was 2.5%. Gas prices remain elevated due to geopolitical tensions.

✓ Fed positioning: Chairman Kevin Warsh signaled at Jackson Hole that "underlying trends have not meaningfully improved" on inflation, leaving open the possibility of rate hikes rather than cuts. Markets now price a 60% chance of a September rate increase.

✓ Consumer debt: Credit card debt hit $1.26 trillion in Q2 2026, with delinquency rates at their highest levels since the Great Recession. Survey data shows 55% of Americans using credit cards for basic necessities.
CONSERVATIVE SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: "Wages growing fastest since the 1980s." Reality: Nominal wage growth has been strong (3.5-4% in some sectors), but what matters is real wages after inflation. When inflation runs at 4.2% and wages grow at 3.5%, workers are losing purchasing power, not gaining it. The 1.9% real wage growth cited by conservative outlets reflects earlier periods when inflation was lower.

✓ Fair Point: Manufacturing has seen solid wage growth and productivity gains. The July jobs loss does reflect some normalization after pandemic distortions, not necessarily a crisis. And wage growth in absolute terms has been respectable compared to the 2010s.
LIBERAL SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: "Job losses mounting." Reality: One month of job losses doesn't constitute a trend. While July was negative and revisions were downward, the overall labor market remains near full employment with a 4.1% unemployment rate. "Mounting" overstates the current trajectory.

✓ Fair Point: The credit card debt data is genuinely alarming and suggests many households are struggling. The gap between wage growth (3.5%) and inflation (4.2%) means real purchasing power is declining. And the Fed's hawkish stance could indeed make borrowing more expensive just as families are already stretched.
THE BIGGER PICTURE:

The economy is in an unusual and uncomfortable position: not quite in recession, but not exactly thriving either. The "meh-conomy" label has merit. Job growth has clearly slowed, inflation remains sticky, and the Fed faces genuine trade-offs with no easy answers. Some workers—particularly in manufacturing and skilled trades—are doing well. Others are struggling with high costs and stagnant opportunities. That's not spin from either side; that's just the complex reality of a $28 trillion economy navigating global shocks.

The Bottom Line: Both wage growth and inflation are real; which one matters more to your household depends on your specific situation. The aggregate data supports neither a celebration nor a catastrophe narrative—just a muddle-through economy with genuine uncertainty ahead.
